title: New Jersey Civics (8th Grade)
description: New Jersey Civics (8th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.correctAnswer: To protect the natural rights of the people
distractors: To give one leader total control of the nation
To collect as much tax money as possible
To force every citizen to join the military
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence says governments are instituted to secure the rights of the people - protecting rights is government's core job, in the nation and in New Jersey.

img.scene: A stately government building with white columns and citizens gathered peacefully on its steps on a sunny day, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Government exists to protect the rights of the people.
img.title: WHY GOVERNMENT EXISTS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Government's job is to guard your rights.
questions.question: What is the main purpose of government, according to the Declaration of Independence?

questions.correctAnswer: Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness
distractors: Free housing, free food, and a guaranteed job
The right to vote at any age
The right to ignore laws you disagree with
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness as unalienable rights - rights people are born with that government may not take away.

img.scene: A sunrise over a peaceful American town with families walking in a park, flags flying gently, hopeful educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Natural rights: life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
img.title: NATURAL RIGHTS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Life, liberty, happiness - born with them all.
questions.question: Which rights are described as 'natural rights' that every person is born with?

questions.correctAnswer: An agreement where people give up some freedoms and agree to follow laws in exchange for protection of their rights
distractors: A contract to buy land from the government
A promise soldiers make when they join the army
A treaty between two foreign countries
questions.explanation: Thinkers like John Locke described government as a social contract: the people consent to be governed, and in return the government protects their rights. If it breaks the contract, the people may change it.

img.scene: Two hands shaking in agreement in front of a colonial town hall, citizens watching approvingly, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The social contract trades some freedom for protection of rights.
img.title: THE SOCIAL CONTRACT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: You follow the rules, government guards your rights - deal!
questions.question: What is the social contract?

questions.correctAnswer: Government gets its power from the permission of the people it governs
distractors: The governor must sign every law twice
Citizens must ask permission before voting
Judges are chosen by the king
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence states that governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed' - the people are the source of all government power.

img.scene: A long line of diverse citizens voting at a colonial meeting house, each raising a hand, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The people give government its power by consenting to it.
img.title: CONSENT OF THE GOVERNED

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Power comes from the people - they consent, government serves.
questions.question: What does 'consent of the governed' mean?

questions.correctAnswer: To announce that the colonies were separating from Britain and explain why
distractors: To set the rules for electing the president
To list the prices of goods in the colonies
To declare war on France
questions.explanation: Adopted on July 4, 1776, the Declaration announced the colonies' independence from Great Britain and listed the grievances against King George III that justified the separation.

img.scene: Colonial delegates in 1776 clothing gathered around a large table in a brick hall, one man presenting a large parchment document, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Declaration announced independence and explained why.
img.title: DECLARING INDEPENDENCE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1776 - the colonies explained their breakup with Britain.
questions.question: Why was the Declaration of Independence written?

questions.correctAnswer: Everyone, including government leaders, must follow the law
distractors: The president makes all the laws alone
Laws apply only to ordinary citizens, not officials
Judges may ignore the Constitution when they choose
questions.explanation: Under the rule of law, no one is above the law - not citizens, not governors, not presidents. It is a founding principle of both the U.S. and New Jersey governments.

img.scene: A balanced scale of justice in front of a courthouse with columns, a diverse crowd and a judge all standing at the same level below it, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Rule of law: the law applies to everyone equally.
img.title: RULE OF LAW

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nobody is above the law - not even the leaders.
questions.question: What does the 'rule of law' mean?

questions.correctAnswer: The idea that the people are the source of all government power
distractors: The idea that the most popular candidate always wins
The rule that states may ignore the Constitution
The power of the Supreme Court to pick the president
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty means the people rule. The Constitution opens with 'We the People' to show that government power comes from the citizens, not from a king or from the government itself.

img.scene: A large crowd of citizens of all ages standing together on a grassy common holding a huge unfurled flag, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Popular sovereignty: the people are the source of power.
img.title: THE PEOPLE RULE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: We the People - the people hold the power.
questions.question: What is popular sovereignty?

questions.correctAnswer: A government whose powers are restricted by a constitution
distractors: A government that meets only once a year
A government with a small army
A government that serves only a few citizens
questions.explanation: In a limited government, a constitution lists what the government may do - and anything not granted is forbidden. Both the U.S. Constitution and the New Jersey Constitution limit government this way.

img.scene: A large stone boundary wall with a gate around a government building, symbolizing clear limits, bright educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A constitution limits what government is allowed to do.
img.title: LIMITED GOVERNMENT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The constitution draws the fence - government stays inside it.
questions.question: What is a limited government?

questions.correctAnswer: Citizens elect representatives to make laws and govern on their behalf
distractors: The president serves for life
Citizens vote directly on every single law
Only landowners may hold office
questions.explanation: In a republic, the people elect representatives - senators, assembly members, members of Congress - who govern on their behalf, instead of voting on every law themselves or being ruled by a monarch.

img.scene: Citizens placing ballots into a wooden ballot box while elected representatives meet inside a hall behind them, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A republic governs through elected representatives.
img.title: A REPUBLIC

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In a republic, you elect people to represent you.
questions.question: The United States is a republic. What does that mean?

questions.correctAnswer: Dividing government into three branches - legislative, executive, and judicial - each with its own duties
distractors: Splitting the country into separate nations
Keeping the military away from the capital city
Giving each state its own currency
questions.explanation: The Constitution divides power among Congress (makes laws), the President (carries out laws), and the courts (interpret laws), so no single part of government controls everything. New Jersey's constitution does the same at the state level.

img.scene: A sturdy tree with three large branches, one holding a scroll, one a shield, one a gavel, bright educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Power is split among legislative, executive, and judicial branches.
img.title: SEPARATION OF POWERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Three branches, three jobs - nobody does it all.
questions.question: What is the separation of powers?

questions.correctAnswer: To let each branch limit the power of the other branches so none becomes too powerful
distractors: To make sure the government budget is always balanced
To check the accuracy of election results
To balance the number of men and women in office
questions.explanation: Checks and balances give each branch tools to restrain the others - a presidential veto, congressional override, court review of laws. The system keeps any one branch from taking over.

img.scene: Three people in a circle each gently holding a rope connected to the others, balanced and steady, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Each branch can limit the others - that keeps power balanced.
img.title: CHECKS AND BALANCES

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Every branch can say 'hold on' to the others.
questions.question: What is the purpose of checks and balances?

questions.correctAnswer: Montesquieu
distractors: King George III
George Washington
Thomas Paine
questions.explanation: The French philosopher Montesquieu argued in 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748) that liberty survives only when legislative, executive, and judicial powers are kept in separate hands - an idea the Framers built into the Constitution.

img.scene: An 18th century philosopher writing at a wooden desk with a quill, candles and stacked books, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Montesquieu championed separating the three powers.
img.title: ENLIGHTENMENT IDEAS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Montesquieu mapped the three branches.
questions.question: Which Enlightenment thinker most influenced the idea of separating government power into three branches?

questions.correctAnswer: The national government could not tax, so it could not pay its debts or fund an army
distractors: The national government had a president who was too powerful
The states were not allowed to have their own governments
The national government controlled all trade inside the states
questions.explanation: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could ask the states for money but could not tax. The new nation could not pay its soldiers or debts, which pushed the states to write the Constitution in 1787.

img.scene: An empty treasury chest with its lid open in a colonial meeting hall, worried delegates looking at it, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Articles gave Congress no power to tax.
img.title: A WEAK FIRST PLAN

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No taxing power meant no money - the Articles were too weak.
questions.question: What was the biggest weakness of the Articles of Confederation?

questions.correctAnswer: It showed that the weak national government could not keep order or respond to a crisis
distractors: It convinced Britain to return the colonies
It elected George Washington as president
It wrote the first ten amendments
questions.explanation: In 1786-87, indebted Massachusetts farmers rebelled and the national government was too weak to respond. The crisis convinced leaders that the Articles of Confederation had to be replaced with a stronger constitution.

img.scene: A crowd of colonial farmers with pitchforks marching toward a courthouse in winter, militia standing watch, tense historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Shays' Rebellion exposed the Articles' weakness.
img.title: A WAKE-UP CALL

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A rebellion the government could not handle sparked a stronger plan.
questions.question: How did Shays' Rebellion help lead to the Constitutional Convention?

questions.correctAnswer: Philadelphia, in 1787
distractors: Trenton, in 1776
New York City, in 1800
Boston, in 1750
questions.explanation: Delegates from twelve states met in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787. They set aside the Articles of Confederation and wrote the U.S. Constitution - and New Jersey's delegates arrived with a famous plan of their own.

img.scene: A grand brick assembly hall in 1787 with horse-drawn carriages outside and delegates in colonial dress arriving, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Convention met in Philadelphia in 1787.
img.title: PHILADELPHIA 1787

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Philadelphia, 1787 - where the Constitution was written.
questions.question: Where and when did the Constitutional Convention meet?

questions.correctAnswer: Congress would have two houses - the House based on population and the Senate with equal representation for every state
distractors: How the president would be elected
Whether slavery would be abolished
Which city would be the capital
questions.explanation: Large states wanted representation by population; small states like New Jersey wanted equal votes. The Great Compromise split the difference: a House based on population and a Senate where every state has two senators.

img.scene: Two groups of colonial delegates shaking hands across a long table in an assembly hall, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The compromise blended population and equality in Congress.
img.title: THE GREAT COMPROMISE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Population in the House, equal in the Senate - compromise!
questions.question: What did the Great Compromise (Connecticut Compromise) settle?

questions.correctAnswer: An agreement that counted three-fifths of a state's enslaved population when setting House seats and taxes
distractors: A rule that three-fifths of states had to approve every law
A promise to free three-fifths of enslaved people
A plan to give three-fifths of western land to Native nations
questions.explanation: Southern states wanted enslaved people counted for representation but not for taxes; Northern states wanted the opposite. The compromise counted three-fifths for both. It protected slavery's political power until the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery in 1865.

img.scene: A somber colonial assembly hall with delegates in serious discussion around a long table, muted evening light, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Enslaved people were counted as three-fifths for House seats and taxes.
img.title: A PAINFUL COMPROMISE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A painful compromise about counting enslaved people - ended only when slavery itself ended.
questions.question: What was the Three-Fifths Compromise?

questions.correctAnswer: They feared a strong national government and demanded a bill of rights to protect individual freedoms
distractors: They wanted the British king to return
They opposed having any president at all
They wanted each state to print its own money
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists worried the Constitution created a national government that was too strong and said nothing about personal rights. Their pressure led to the promise of a Bill of Rights, added in 1791.

img.scene: Colonial citizens debating passionately in a town square, one holding up a large blank parchment, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Anti-Federalists feared strong central power and demanded a bill of rights.
img.title: THE GREAT DEBATE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Anti-Federalists demanded rights in writing - and got the Bill of Rights.
questions.question: Why did the Anti-Federalists oppose the new Constitution at first?

questions.correctAnswer: A series of essays written to persuade the states to ratify the Constitution
distractors: The official journal kept by the Constitutional Convention
A newspaper published by the British government
The first laws passed by Congress
questions.explanation: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote 85 essays under the name 'Publius' explaining and defending the Constitution. New Jersey's neighbor across the Hudson saw the fiercest ratification debate of all.

img.scene: A writer at a candlelit desk with a quill, stacked pamphlets beside him, 18th century study, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Federalist Papers argued for ratifying the Constitution.
img.title: PERSUADING THE STATES

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Hamilton, Madison, and Jay wrote essays to sell the Constitution.
questions.question: What were the Federalist Papers?

questions.correctAnswer: Nine of the thirteen states
distractors: All thirteen states
Seven of the thirteen states
A majority of the people in a national vote
questions.explanation: Article VII set the bar at nine states. New Hampshire became the ninth in June 1788, but the new government needed the big states - and small-state New Jersey ratified early and unanimously, third overall.

img.scene: A map-like view of the thirteen colonies along the Atlantic coast with small flags on nine of them, historical educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Nine of thirteen states had to ratify for the Constitution to take effect.
img.title: NINE STATES TO START

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Nine states made it official.
questions.question: How many states had to ratify the Constitution before it could take effect?

questions.correctAnswer: Popular sovereignty - the government's power comes from the people
distractors: The president is the source of all power
Only people who own land may govern
The states created the people
questions.explanation: The Preamble's first words announce that the people, not a king or a government, hold the ultimate authority - and that the people established the Constitution itself.

img.scene: A diverse crowd of citizens standing together beneath a grand archway at sunrise, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Preamble opens by putting the people in charge.
img.title: WE THE PEOPLE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 'We the People' - it starts with us.
questions.question: The Constitution begins with 'We the People of the United States.' What idea do those words express?

questions.correctAnswer: The legislative branch - Congress
distractors: The executive branch - the President
The judicial branch - the courts
The military
questions.explanation: Article I establishes Congress and lists its powers. Article II creates the presidency, and Article III creates the federal courts.

img.scene: A grand domed capitol building with rows of seats visible through its open doors, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Article I creates Congress, the lawmaking branch.
img.title: ARTICLE I: CONGRESS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Article I - Congress comes first.
questions.question: Which branch of government does Article I of the Constitution create?

questions.correctAnswer: The Constitution and federal laws are the supreme law of the land, above state laws when they conflict
distractors: The president is supreme over the courts
State laws always override federal laws
The Supreme Court may write new laws
questions.explanation: The supremacy clause makes the U.S. Constitution the highest law in the country. When a state law conflicts with a valid federal law, the federal law wins - in New Jersey and every other state.

img.scene: A tall stone pyramid of layered blocks with a glowing parchment resting on the top layer, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Federal law outranks state law when the two conflict.
img.title: SUPREME LAW OF THE LAND

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Constitution sits at the top - no state law outranks it.
questions.question: What does the supremacy clause (Article VI) establish?

questions.correctAnswer: It stretches Congress's power to make laws needed to carry out its listed powers
distractors: It lets Congress stretch the length of its sessions
It stretches the president's term during wars
It allows states to stretch their borders
questions.explanation: Article I gives Congress power to make all laws 'necessary and proper' for executing its enumerated powers. Like elastic, it stretches to cover implied powers - such as creating a national bank, as upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland.

img.scene: A long elastic band being stretched between a capitol building and a toolbox of government tools, playful educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The elastic clause lets Congress pass laws needed to use its listed powers.
img.title: THE ELASTIC CLAUSE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The elastic clause stretches Congress's reach to get its jobs done.
questions.question: Why is the 'necessary and proper' clause also called the elastic clause?

questions.correctAnswer: Enumerated powers are listed for the federal government; reserved powers are kept by the states and the people
distractors: Enumerated powers belong to the states; reserved powers belong to the president
Enumerated powers are about money; reserved powers are about the military
They are two names for exactly the same powers
questions.explanation: The Constitution enumerates (lists) federal powers like declaring war and coining money. The Tenth Amendment reserves everything else to the states or the people - which is why states run schools, elections, and local police.

img.scene: Two columns of stone pillars, a tall set in a capital city and a set spread across small towns, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Enumerated = listed for the federal government; reserved = kept by states.
img.title: TWO SETS OF POWERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Listed powers go to Washington; the rest stays with the states.
questions.question: What is the difference between enumerated powers and reserved powers?

questions.correctAnswer: Powers not given to the federal government, and not denied to the states, belong to the states or to the people
distractors: The federal government may take any power it wants
States may nullify any federal law they dislike
Citizens have a right to a free education from Congress
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment protects federalism: Washington has only the powers the Constitution grants, and everything else is reserved - which is why New Jersey runs its own schools, roads, and state courts.

img.scene: A stone tablet-like monument standing in a town square with a small crowd reading it, bright educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Tenth Amendment reserves unlisted powers to states and the people.
img.title: THE TENTH AMENDMENT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Not granted to Washington? Reserved for the states.
questions.question: What does the Tenth Amendment say?

questions.correctAnswer: Taxation - both may collect taxes from the people
distractors: Declaring war
Coining money
Granting titles of nobility
questions.explanation: Concurrent powers are shared: both levels of government tax, build roads, and run courts. Only the federal government may declare war or coin money - those are enumerated federal powers.

img.scene: Two cash registers side by side in a market, one under a national flag and one under a state flag, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Concurrent powers, like taxation, are shared by both levels.
img.title: SHARED POWERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Taxes come from both levels - that is a concurrent power.
questions.question: Which of these is a concurrent power, shared by the federal and state governments?

questions.correctAnswer: Two-thirds of Congress proposes an amendment, and three-fourths of the states ratify it
distractors: The president proposes it and half the states approve
A majority of voters in one national election approves it
The Supreme Court proposes it and Congress approves by majority
questions.explanation: Article V makes amending deliberately hard: proposal takes two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention), and ratification takes three-fourths of the states. Only 27 amendments have made it through.

img.scene: A long staircase climbing toward a glowing parchment, with many state flags planted along the steps, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Amendments need two-thirds to propose and three-fourths of states to ratify.
img.title: CHANGING THE CONSTITUTION

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two-thirds proposes, three-fourths ratifies - no shortcuts.
questions.question: How is the U.S. Constitution amended?

questions.correctAnswer: States must respect the official acts, records, and court decisions of other states
distractors: States must have identical laws about driving and marriage
Citizens receive full military protection in every state
States may not charge taxes to visitors
questions.explanation: Article IV's full faith and credit clause makes the union work as one country: a driver's license, marriage certificate, or court judgment from New Jersey is honored in Florida or California too.

img.scene: A bridge connecting two river towns, travelers with documents walking across freely, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: States honor each other's records, acts, and court decisions.
img.title: FULL FAITH AND CREDIT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Your New Jersey license works in every state - full faith and credit.
questions.question: What does the full faith and credit clause require of the states?

questions.correctAnswer: Passing ex post facto laws - punishing someone for an act that was legal when it was done
distractors: Collecting income taxes
Declaring a state of emergency
Regulating businesses
questions.explanation: Article I forbids both Congress and the states from passing ex post facto laws and bills of attainder, and protects habeas corpus - limits that keep governments from punishing people unfairly or retroactively.

img.scene: A clock with its hands being held from turning backward by a stone barrier, symbolic educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Governments may not punish past acts that were legal when done.
img.title: LIMITS ON GOVERNMENT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No ex post facto - you cannot be punished under a law written later.
questions.question: Which action is forbidden to both the federal and state governments by the Constitution?

questions.correctAnswer: Two years, and the number of representatives depends on each state's population
distractors: Six years, and every state gets the same number
Four years, and the president appoints them
Life terms, like Supreme Court justices
questions.explanation: House members face the voters every two years, keeping them close to the people. Seats are apportioned by population after each census - New Jersey currently sends 12 representatives to the House.

img.scene: A large semicircular chamber filled with many rows of desks and seats, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: House: two-year terms, seats by population.
img.title: THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House members answer to voters every two years.
questions.question: How long is a U.S. Representative's term, and how are House seats divided among the states?

questions.correctAnswer: Six years, and every state elects exactly two senators
distractors: Two years, and states elect senators by population
Four years, and the governor appoints them
Ten years, and each state elects one
questions.explanation: Equal Senate representation was the small states' win in the Great Compromise - New Jersey's idea of equality survives there. Six-year staggered terms give the Senate stability.

img.scene: A semicircular chamber with one hundred desks arranged in arcs, dignified educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Senate: six-year terms, two per state.
img.title: THE SENATE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Two senators per state - small states' equality lives here.
questions.question: How long is a U.S. Senator's term, and how many senators does each state elect?

questions.correctAnswer: Representative: 25; Senator: 30; President: 35
distractors: Representative: 18; Senator: 21; President: 25
Representative: 30; Senator: 35; President: 40
Representative: 21; Senator: 25; President: 30
questions.explanation: The Constitution sets minimum ages that rise with the office: 25 for the House, 30 for the Senate, and 35 for the presidency - along with citizenship and residency rules for each.

img.scene: Three ascending stone steps, each topped with a different chair - a small desk chair, a larger chair, and a grand chair, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Minimum ages rise with the office: 25, 30, 35.
img.title: AGE REQUIREMENTS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 25 for the House, 30 for the Senate, 35 for the top job.
questions.question: What are the minimum ages for serving as a U.S. Representative, a U.S. Senator, and President?

questions.correctAnswer: Declaring war
distractors: Commanding the army in battle
Appointing Supreme Court justices
Granting pardons for federal crimes
questions.explanation: Only Congress can declare war and raise and fund the military. The president commands the armed forces, appoints justices (with Senate consent), and issues pardons - the branches check each other even in war powers.

img.scene: A chamber of legislators voting by raised hands beneath a large flag, solemn educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Only Congress can declare war.
img.title: WAR POWERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Congress declares war; the president commands the troops.
questions.question: Under the Constitution, declaring war is a power of which part of government?

questions.correctAnswer: It passes both houses of Congress in the same form and is signed by the president
distractors: It passes the House only and becomes law automatically
The Supreme Court approves its wording
The governor of each state signs it
questions.explanation: A bill must clear committees, pass the House and Senate in identical form, and reach the president's desk. The same path - legislature plus governor - applies to laws in Trenton.

img.scene: A parchment traveling along a path through a chamber, a second chamber, and onto a polished executive desk with a pen waiting, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Both houses pass it, then the president signs it.
img.title: HOW A BILL BECOMES LAW

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: House, Senate, president's pen - that is the journey of a bill.
questions.question: How does a federal bill become a law?

questions.correctAnswer: Congress may override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses
distractors: The bill dies and can never be introduced again
The Supreme Court decides whether it becomes law
The bill automatically becomes law in ten days
questions.explanation: The veto is the president's check on Congress; the two-thirds override is Congress's check right back. New Jersey's governor and legislature play the same tug-of-war in Trenton.

img.scene: A large wooden stamp resting on a desk while legislators in a chamber stand to vote, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: A two-thirds vote in both houses overrides a presidential veto.
img.title: THE VETO AND OVERRIDE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Veto slows a bill - two-thirds brings it back.
questions.question: What happens when the president vetoes a bill?

questions.correctAnswer: Confirming presidential appointments and approving treaties
distractors: Writing the federal budget alone
Commanding the armed forces
Trying citizens accused of crimes
questions.explanation: The Senate alone confirms cabinet officers, ambassadors, and judges, and approves treaties by a two-thirds vote - the Senate's 'advice and consent' role. New Jersey's Senate plays the same confirming role for the governor's nominees.

img.scene: A panel of seated senators in a chamber listening to a nominee at a table before them, educational illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Senate confirms appointments and approves treaties.
img.title: ADVICE AND CONSENT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The president nominates; the Senate decides.
questions.question: Which responsibilities belong only to the U.S. Senate?

questions.correctAnswer: Congress may create a national bank, because a bank is a necessary and proper way to manage federal money
distractors: States may tax federal banks out of existence

Defendants never have to appear in court
